title: Maximal extension and conformal compactification
one_line_summary: Defines maximal and geodesically complete spacetimes, builds Kruskal's maximal analytic extension of Schwarzschild by reparametrising the two radial null coordinates, reads off the four-region Kruskal diagram and the Einstein-Rosen bridge, then invents Penrose diagrams by conformally squeezing Minkowski spacetime into a finite diamond of the Einstein static universe, and ends with the Kruskal and collapse Penrose diagrams and the idea of a trapped surface.
role_in_book: Second chapter of Part D. Chapter 17 showed that the Schwarzschild exterior can be continued through r = 2m in two inequivalent ways (advanced and retarded Eddington-Finkelstein charts, black hole and white hole). This short, diagram-heavy chapter asks whether those continuations can be carried further, answers with the unique Kruskal extension, and then supplies the global tool (conformal compactification and Penrose diagrams, with scri and the points i+, i0, i-) that Chapter 19 uses for Reissner-Nordstrom, Chapter 20 for Kerr and the singularity theorems, and Part F for the conformal structure of cosmological models. It also plants trapped surfaces as the ingredient behind the singularity theorems of §20.13.

assumed_background.topic: Schwarzschild line element in geometric units, meaning of m and the surface r = 2m
Advanced and retarded Eddington-Finkelstein null coordinates v and w, black hole and white hole extensions, their space-time diagrams
Distinction between coordinate and intrinsic (curvature) singularities
Affine parameter along geodesics and geodesic equation
Conformally related metrics; every two-dimensional metric is conformally flat; conformal rescaling preserves null geodesics
Light cones, causal structure and spacetime diagrams in special relativity
Einstein static universe as a solution with cosmological constant
Hyperbolas, inverse tangent, and implicit functions
Changing variables in a line element (chain rule for differentials)
Embedding a curved 2-surface in flat 3-space to visualise its intrinsic geometry
Manifold topology basics: spheres S^2 and S^3, cylinders, compact versus non-compact

learning_objectives: Reader can state what it means for a spacetime to be maximal and to be geodesically complete, and explain why complete implies maximal but not conversely, using Minkowski and Kruskal as examples.
Reader can rewrite the Schwarzschild metric in double null coordinates (v, w) and explain why the (t, r) 2-metric is automatically conformally flat.
Reader can explain why reparametrising v and w separately keeps the 2-metric in conformally flat null form, and carry out Kruskal's exponential choice to obtain (18.8)-(18.9).

Reader can sketch the Kruskal diagram, locate the horizons, the spacelike future and past singularities, lines of constant r and t, and identify regions I, II, I', II' with the exterior, black hole, second exterior and white hole.

Reader can describe the Einstein-Rosen bridge on the t' = 0 slice, explain how the throat evolves and pinches off, and distinguish it from a single-universe Schwarzschild wormhole with the same local geometry.

Reader can explain the physical/unphysical metric construction, why a conformal factor leaves light cones and causal structure unchanged, and how arctan-type maps bring infinity to finite coordinate values.
Reader can carry out the conformal compactification of Minkowski spacetime step by step to (18.27) and recognise the result as a finite diamond on the Einstein static universe cylinder.
Reader can name and locate i+, i-, i0, scri+ and scri- on the Minkowski Penrose diagram and state where timelike, null and spacelike geodesics begin and end.
Reader can read the Kruskal Penrose diagram: which infinities belong to regions I and I', where ingoing and outgoing radial light rays from any point end up, and why region II is inescapable.
Reader can define a trapped surface via the areas of the two families of wave fronts from an illuminated 2-sphere, classify spheres in regions I, II and II', and explain why closedness is essential.
Reader can explain why the Penrose diagram of realistic spherical collapse contains only parts of regions I and II and no second universe or white hole.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, coordinate-driven chapter whose real content lives in its diagrams. Each global statement is obtained by choosing clever coordinates for the radial 2-space, then drawn: first a Kruskal diagram with straight 45-degree null lines, then embedding pictures of the t' = constant slices, then Penrose diagrams. Minkowski space is used as a fully worked prototype before the harder Kruskal compactification is simply stated with its picture. Many algebraic steps are deferred to the exercises, and the chapter closes on physical interpretation (trapped surfaces, collapse) rather than on computation.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: the Eddington-Finkelstein charts continue Schwarzschild past r = 2m; can the manifold be continued even further?
Make the question precise: define maximal and geodesically complete spacetimes, note Minkowski is complete, Schwarzschild and EF are not maximal, Kruskal is maximal and unique but incomplete.
Model: put both advanced and retarded null coordinates on the radial 2-space, observe conformal flatness, and isolate the freedom to relabel each null family separately.
Formalism: Kruskal's exponential relabelling gives a metric with a regular conformal factor, r defined implicitly by a hyperbola equation.
Picture: Kruskal diagram with four regions, two spacelike singularities, horizons as asymptotes, and an infalling particle whose signals escape only before crossing r = 2m.

Interpretation: embed the t' = 0 slice to reveal the Einstein-Rosen bridge, follow its time evolution to pinch-off, and contrast with a wormhole of different topology to stress that field equations fix local geometry only.
New question: the Kruskal diagram still hides infinity. Introduce a physical and an unphysical metric related by a conformal factor that preserves null geodesics.
Prototype computation: compactify Minkowski with null coordinates and arctan, arriving at the Einstein static universe metric on a finite diamond.
Classify the conformal boundary (scri+-, i+-, i0) and state where each type of geodesic starts and ends; define the Penrose diagram.
Application: state the Kruskal compactification and present its Penrose diagram, reading off the fate of radial light rays in each region.
Physical payoff: illuminate a 2-sphere to define trapped surfaces, relate them to singularity theorems, and show the Penrose diagram of a collapsing star.
signature_moves: Frames extension as a sharpened question with formal definitions (maximal versus geodesically complete) before any coordinates are chosen.
Uses the residual freedom v -> v'(v), w -> w'(w) of double null coordinates as the single idea behind both the Kruskal chart and the Penrose compactification.
Treats Minkowski spacetime as a worked prototype for conformal compactification, then transfers the recipe to Kruskal with details omitted.
Constantly reminds that each point of a 2D diagram stands for a 2-sphere, and recovers suppressed dimensions by rotating diagrams about an axis (Figs 18.2, 18.3, 18.8).
Separates local geometry from topology by showing two embeddings of the same slice geometry (bridge versus folded-sheet wormhole).
Defines trapped surfaces operationally through the areas of the two envelopes of Huygens wavelets from an illuminated sphere, then gives a counterexample to show closedness matters.
Leaves several decisive steps (metric transformations, drawing constant-coordinate curves, the fate of observers from I and I', what collapse does to I' and II') to short exercises.

sections.title: Maximal analytic extensions
sections.summary: Recalls that the Eddington-Finkelstein charts extend Schwarzschild inward because radial infall passes smoothly through r = 2m, and asks whether further extension is possible. Makes this precise: a spacetime is maximal if every geodesic either runs to infinite affine parameter both ways or ends at an intrinsic singularity, and geodesically complete if every geodesic runs to infinite affine parameter. Minkowski space is complete; Schwarzschild and both EF charts are not maximal; Kruskal's extension is maximal and unique yet incomplete because of its singularities, and is built by straightening both families of radial null geodesics at once.
key_moves: Uses the geodesic behaviour at r = 2m (radial timelike geodesics continue to r = 0) as evidence that the Schwarzschild chart is incomplete.
Replaces the vague question 'can we extend further?' by the affine-parameter criterion for maximality.
Notes the logical relation: completeness implies maximality, but a maximal spacetime may still have geodesics ending at singularities.
Announces the strategy for Kruskal: straighten ingoing and outgoing radial null geodesics simultaneously (each EF chart straightens only one family).

sections.title: The Kruskal solution
sections.summary: Writes Schwarzschild in the double null coordinates v = t + r*, w = t - r* with the tortoise coordinate r*, so the radial 2-metric is (1 - 2m/r) dv dw and hence conformally flat. Any separate relabelling of v and w preserves this null form, giving a general F^2 (dt'^2 - dx'^2). Kruskal's choice v' = exp(v/4m), w' = -exp(-w/4m) yields a conformal factor F^2 = (16m^2/r) exp(-r/2m) that is regular at r = 2m, with r fixed implicitly by t'^2 - x'^2 = -(r - 2m) exp(r/2m). The resulting diagram has 45-degree light cones everywhere, r = constant hyperbolae, horizons along the diagonals, spacelike future and past singularities at r = 0, and four regions: I (exterior), II (black hole), II' (white hole) and a surprising second exterior I'.
key_moves: Combine the advanced and retarded EF null coordinates into one chart (18.1)-(18.4).
Invoke the theorem that every 2D metric is conformally flat, exhibited by t~ = (v+w)/2, x~ = (v-w)/2.
Observe that v -> v'(v), w -> w'(w) is the most general change keeping the 2-metric in conformally flat double null form.
Choose exponentials so that the factor (1 - 2m/r) is cancelled by the Jacobian, leaving a factor regular at r = 2m, (18.6)-(18.9).
Read global structure off (18.8): each r labels a pair of hyperbolae; r = 2m gives the diagonals; r = 0 gives two spacelike boundary hyperbolae.
Match regions to earlier charts: I and II are the advanced EF chart, I and II' the retarded EF chart, I' is new.
Trace the radial timelike geodesic drawn from (r = 4m, t' = 0) into region II: the outward signals it emits escape only while it is still outside r = 2m.

sections.title: The Einstein-Rosen bridge
sections.summary: Restores the suppressed 2-spheres by examining the spatial slice t' = 0. Along the x' axis r falls from infinity to a minimum of 2m at x' = 0 and rises again, so the equatorial slice embeds as two asymptotically flat sheets joined by a throat of radius 2m: the Einstein-Rosen bridge. At later Kruskal times the throat narrows, pinches off where the slice meets r = 0 and leaves two separate universes each with a singularity; the evolution is time symmetric. The authors flag the physical status of region I' as open, emphasise that the field equations fix local geometry but not topology, and show a wormhole embedding that joins two distant parts of one universe with identical local geometry.
concepts: dynamical pinch-off of the Einstein-Rosen bridge
key_moves: Induce the spatial metric (18.10) on t' = 0 and restrict to the equator (18.11).
Use (18.8) with t' = 0 to see r has a minimum 2m at x' = 0: two exteriors meet at a minimal sphere.
Embed the 2-geometry in flat 3-space to draw the bridge (Fig. 18.2).
Follow t' = constant slices: the minimal radius shrinks below 2m, reaches zero at the singularity, then the sheets separate (Fig. 18.3).
Show a second, topologically different embedding of the same local geometry (Fig. 18.4) to separate geometry from topology.
Motivate the next tool: the Kruskal diagram does not show infinity.

sections.title: Penrose diagram for Minkowski space-time
sections.summary: Introduces a physical metric g and an unphysical metric Omega^2 g; because conformally related metrics share null geodesics, the unphysical metric has the same light cones and causal structure, while a suitable Omega can bring infinity to finite coordinates via arctan-type maps. For Minkowski space, null coordinates v = t + r, w = t - r (with v >= w) are squashed by p = arctan v, q = arctan w; the metric becomes a conformal factor times the unphysical metric 4 dp dq - sin^2(p - q) dOmega^2. With t' = p + q, r' = p - q this is the Einstein static universe metric, so all of Minkowski space maps onto a finite diamond of that cylinder. Its boundary consists of the null surfaces scri+ and scri- and the points i+, i0, i-, which serve as the endpoints of timelike, null and spacelike geodesics. The picture of this compactified spacetime is the Penrose diagram, and the method extends to Penrose's simple spacetimes.
key_moves: State the conformal rescaling (18.12) and its key property: light cones are unchanged.
Show arctan as the model map from an infinite line to a finite interval (Fig. 18.5).
Write Minkowski in null coordinates (18.15) with the half-plane constraint v >= w (18.16).
Apply p = arctan v, q = arctan w and factor out 1/4 sec^2 p sec^2 q to expose the unphysical metric (18.20)-(18.21).
Rotate to t' = p + q, r' = p - q to recognise the Einstein static universe (18.27) on the restricted range (18.24)-(18.26).
Picture the ESU as a cylinder via an embedding in 5D flat space and shade the diamond that is Minkowski space (Fig. 18.7).
List the boundary pieces in (p, q) and assign each as the start or end point of a class of geodesics (Fig. 18.8), with a warning that accelerated curves need not obey the rules.

Define the Penrose diagram and draw constant-t curves (spacelike slices meeting at i0) and constant-r curves (timelike sphere histories from i- to i+) in it, with p = const and q = const as the -45 and +45 degree radial light rays (Fig. 18.9).

sections.title: Penrose diagram for the Kruskal solution
sections.summary: Compactifies Kruskal by applying arctan to the Kruskal null coordinates scaled by (2m)^(1/2), states coordinate ranges, omits the computation and presents the Penrose diagram: a flattened hexagon in which regions I and I' each have their own i+, i0, i-, scri+ and scri-, and horizontal wavy edges mark the future and past singularities. From a point outside r = 2m the outgoing radial light ray reaches scri+ while the ingoing one hits the future singularity; inside r = 2m both hit the singularity.
concepts: Penrose diagram of the Kruskal spacetime
key_moves: Reuse the Minkowski recipe: arctan of null coordinates, here v'' = arctan(v'/(2m)^(1/2)), w'' = arctan(w'/(2m)^(1/2)).
Read causal fate from 45-degree lines in the diagram rather than from equations.
Point out that each asymptotic region carries a complete set of conformal infinities.

sections.title: Trapped surfaces and the Penrose diagram of collapse (end of §18.5)
sections.summary: Returns to the 2-spheres behind each diagram point. Light flashed from every point of a sphere S0 produces two envelopes, one outgoing and one ingoing. In region I the outgoing envelope has larger area and the ingoing one smaller; in region II both envelopes have smaller area than S0. A closed 2-surface whose light rays converge in both directions is a trapped surface; spheres in II' are time-reversed trapped surfaces. Trapped surfaces are the key input to singularity theorems. The authors defend Penrose's term over 'closed trapped surface' with a Minkowski counterexample: the intersection of two past light cones is convergent in both directions but is not closed and not trapped. The chapter ends with the Penrose diagram of a collapsing spherical star.
concepts: Penrose diagram of spherical gravitational collapse
key_moves: Replace a diagram point by its 2-sphere and apply Huygens' construction to get two wave fronts (Fig. 18.11).
Compare areas of the ingoing and outgoing wave fronts with the original sphere to diagnose trapping.
Classify spheres: normal in I, trapped in II, anti-trapped in II'.
Use a Minkowski counterexample to argue that convergence alone is not trapping; compactness is required.
Show the collapse Penrose diagram, where the star interior replaces the second exterior and white hole (Fig. 18.12).

concepts.name: maximal spacetime
concepts.definition: A manifold with affine or metric geometry in which every geodesic, followed in both directions, either continues to arbitrarily large affine parameter or ends at an intrinsic singularity; nothing can be added to it.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to turn the question 'can the Eddington-Finkelstein charts be extended further?' into a precise criterion based on the affine parameter of geodesics.
concepts.notes: The book's criterion is the geodesic one; modern treatments define maximality as inextendibility of the manifold (no isometric embedding as a proper open subset of a larger spacetime).

concepts.name: geodesic completeness
concepts.definition: A spacetime is geodesically complete if every geodesic can be extended to infinite affine parameter in both directions. Complete spacetimes are maximal; maximal spacetimes need not be complete.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined immediately after maximality as the special case with no singular endpoints; Minkowski is the trivial example, Kruskal the example of maximal but incomplete.

concepts.name: intrinsic singularity
concepts.definition: A place where the geometry itself breaks down (for Schwarzschild, curvature invariants blow up at r = 0), which cannot be removed by any change of coordinates; geodesics that reach it cannot be continued.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from §17.2 as the allowed way for a geodesic to end in a maximal spacetime; r = 0 becomes the two hyperbolic boundaries of the Kruskal diagram.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A place where a particular chart fails (metric components vanish or blow up, or coordinates stop being one-to-one) although the geometry is perfectly regular there, such as r = 2m in Schwarzschild coordinates or r' = 0, pi and theta = 0, pi on the Einstein static universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned when listing the ESU coordinate ranges, where the poles of the 3-sphere chart are called coordinate singularities; implicitly behind the whole Kruskal construction.

concepts.name: maximal analytic extension
concepts.definition: The process of continuing a spacetime known on one chart to the largest spacetime into which it embeds with an analytic metric; for Schwarzschild the result is unique and is the Kruskal spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as the goal of the chapter after the EF charts were found to be non-maximal; Kruskal is credited with finding the unique answer.

concepts.name: Kruskal extension
concepts.definition: The unique maximal analytic extension of the vacuum Schwarzschild geometry: a spacetime with two asymptotically flat exterior regions, a black hole region, a white hole region, horizons at r = 2m, and spacelike singularities at r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Built in §18.2 by straightening both families of radial null geodesics, then interpreted with the Kruskal diagram, embedding diagrams and finally a Penrose diagram.
concepts.notes: Maximal but not geodesically complete. The book does not name Szekeres, who found the same extension independently.

concepts.name: Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
concepts.definition: Charts for Schwarzschild built on the ingoing null coordinate v = t + r* (advanced, covering exterior plus black hole) or the outgoing null coordinate w = t - r* (retarded, covering exterior plus white hole), in which one family of radial light rays is straight and the metric is regular at r = 2m.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 17 as the partial extensions that motivate the search for a maximal one; the Kruskal diagram shows each as a pair of its four regions.
formulas: v = t + r^*,\quad w = t - r^*

concepts.name: double null coordinates
aliases: advanced and retarded null coordinates used together
concepts.definition: Coordinates (v, w) on a two-dimensional Lorentzian space whose coordinate lines are both families of null curves, so the 2-metric takes the form f dv dw with no dv^2 or dw^2 terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Used first on the Schwarzschild radial 2-space (18.1) and then on Minkowski space (18.13)-(18.15); both Kruskal and Penrose constructions start from them.

concepts.name: tortoise coordinate
concepts.definition: The radial function r* = r + 2m ln(r - 2m) (for r > 2m) chosen so that radial light rays satisfy t = +-r* + constant; it tends to minus infinity as r approaches 2m, reflecting the infinite coordinate time taken to reach the horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in passing when writing v and w symmetrically as t +- r*.
concepts.notes: The logarithm's argument should be made dimensionless, e.g. ln(r/2m - 1); the constant shift is harmless but matters for the numerical scale of Kruskal coordinates.

concepts.name: conformal flatness of two-dimensional metrics
concepts.definition: Every two-dimensional metric can locally be written as a function times a flat metric; for a Lorentzian 2-space this is realised by double null coordinates, ds^2 = F^2 (dt^2 - dx^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked from §6.13 to justify that the Schwarzschild radial 2-space (18.5) is conformally flat, made explicit with t~ = (v+w)/2, x~ = (v-w)/2.

concepts.name: null coordinate reparametrisation freedom
concepts.definition: In double null form f dv dw, replacing v by any monotonic function v'(v) and w by any w'(w) keeps the metric of the form f' dv' dw'; only the conformal factor changes. This freedom can be spent to make the factor regular or to make coordinate ranges finite.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the most general transformation preserving the conformally flat null form; Kruskal's exponentials and Penrose's arctans are both particular uses of it.
concepts.notes: This is the unifying idea of the chapter even though the book never names it.

concepts.name: Kruskal coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates t' = (v' + w')/2, x' = (v' - w')/2 built from v' = exp(v/4m), w' = -exp(-w/4m); in them radial light rays are 45-degree lines, the metric factor is regular at r = 2m, and r is defined implicitly by t'^2 - x'^2 = -(r - 2m) exp(r/2m).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived as Kruskal's specific choice of null reparametrisation that cancels the zero of (1 - 2m/r) with the Jacobian of the exponential.
concepts.notes: As defined, v' > 0 and w' < 0 cover only region I; the extension consists in letting (t', x') range over all values with r > 0.

concepts.name: Kruskal diagram
concepts.definition: The (t', x') plane of the Kruskal spacetime with angular directions suppressed: light cones are 45 degrees everywhere, r = constant curves are hyperbolae, Schwarzschild t = constant curves are straight lines through the origin, the diagonals are the horizons, and r = 0 is a pair of spacelike hyperbolae bounding the spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as Fig. 18.1 immediately after the metric, with an infalling particle and its escaping signals.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: The null surface r = 2m that separates events that can send signals to distant observers from those that cannot; in Kruskal coordinates it is the pair of diagonal lines t' = +-x', which cross at the bifurcation 2-sphere.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the asymptotes of the r = constant hyperbolae in Fig. 18.1 and as the diagonals of the Penrose diagram Fig. 18.10.

concepts.name: black hole region
concepts.definition: The region of the Kruskal spacetime inside the future horizon, from which every future-directed causal curve reaches the future singularity and no signal reaches the exterior.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified as region II of the Kruskal diagram, matching the interior part of the advanced EF chart; its inescapability is tied to the spacelike nature of the future singularity and later to trapped surfaces.

concepts.name: white hole region
concepts.definition: The time reverse of the black hole region: the region inside the past horizon, emerging from the past singularity, from which everything must leave and which nothing can enter from outside.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified as region II' of the Kruskal diagram, matching the interior part of the retarded EF chart; its 2-spheres are time-reversed trapped surfaces.

concepts.name: second asymptotically flat region
concepts.definition: A second exterior Schwarzschild region, geometrically identical to region I and asymptotically flat, that the maximal extension forces to exist; it is causally disconnected from region I, though observers from both can meet inside the black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the surprise of the Kruskal diagram; its physical significance is described as an open question, and it disappears in the collapse diagram.

concepts.name: spacelike singularity
concepts.definition: A singular boundary whose locus is spacelike, so that it lies to the future (or past) of every nearby event rather than at a place; a future spacelike singularity cannot be avoided once inside the region it bounds.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated for the future r = 0 hyperbola in Fig. 18.1, whose spacelike character makes it unavoidable in region II; in the Penrose diagram both singularities become horizontal wavy edges.

concepts.name: Einstein-Rosen bridge
concepts.definition: The geometry of the Kruskal spacetime on the slice t' = 0: two asymptotically flat spatial sheets joined through a minimal 2-sphere of area 16 pi m^2 (r = 2m).
concepts.how_introduced: Found by inducing the metric on t' = 0, noting that r has a minimum at x' = 0, and embedding the equatorial section in flat 3-space (Fig. 18.2).

concepts.name: embedding diagram
concepts.definition: A picture of the intrinsic geometry of a 2D spatial section obtained by finding a surface in flat 3D Euclidean space with the same induced line element; only the surface's intrinsic distances carry meaning.
concepts.how_introduced: Used on the equatorial section of t' = 0 (and later slices) to visualise the bridge and the wormhole; no explicit embedding function is given.
concepts.notes: For Schwarzschild the surface is z = +-(8m(r - 2m))^(1/2), not stated in this chapter.

concepts.name: dynamical pinch-off of the Einstein-Rosen bridge
concepts.definition: On successive Kruskal slices t' = constant the throat radius drops below 2m, reaches zero when the slice touches the future singularity, and the two sheets then separate, each with its own singularity; the same happens toward the past by time symmetry. The throat closes too fast for any signal to cross from I to I'.
concepts.how_introduced: Described qualitatively and summarised in the seven-panel strip Fig. 18.3, with the instruction to rotate each profile to rebuild the surface.
concepts.notes: The book places pinch-off at t' = +-1; with (18.8) as printed it occurs at t' = +-(2m)^(1/2).

concepts.name: local geometry versus global topology
aliases: topology not fixed by field equations
concepts.definition: Einstein's equations are local differential equations: they constrain the metric near each point but do not determine how regions are glued together, so different global manifolds can share the same local geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised while discussing whether region I' is physical, illustrated by a wormhole embedding with the same local slice geometry as the bridge.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild wormhole
concepts.definition: A spatial geometry locally identical to the Einstein-Rosen bridge but with the two asymptotic sheets identified as distant parts of one universe, so the throat is a shortcut between them.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown as an alternative embedding (Fig. 18.4) to make the geometry-topology point, then explicitly not pursued.
concepts.notes: Not a solution of Einstein's equations globally without further identifications or matter; the book leaves it as an illustration.

concepts.name: conformal transformation
concepts.definition: Replacing a metric g_ab by Omega^2 g_ab with a positive function Omega; angles and the null cone at each point are unchanged but lengths and curvature change.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the device for pulling infinity to a finite place, with Omega the conformal factor.

concepts.name: physical and unphysical metrics
concepts.definition: In conformal compactification the true spacetime metric is called physical and the rescaled metric Omega^2 g_ab, which is regular on the added boundary at infinity, is called unphysical; only its causal structure is to be trusted.
concepts.how_introduced: Named at the start of §18.4 when the construction is set up.

concepts.name: conformal invariance of null geodesics
concepts.definition: Two conformally related metrics have the same null geodesics (as unparametrised curves), hence the same light cones and the same causal relations between events.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from Exercise 6.29 as the reason a conformally compactified picture faithfully displays causal structure.
concepts.notes: Affine parametrisation of null geodesics does change under rescaling; timelike and spacelike geodesics are not preserved.

concepts.name: compactifying coordinate map
concepts.definition: A monotonic function such as arctan that maps an infinite coordinate range onto a finite interval, used on null coordinates so that points at infinity acquire finite coordinate values.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown graphically (Fig. 18.5) and then applied to Minkowski null coordinates and to Kruskal null coordinates.

concepts.name: conformal compactification
concepts.definition: Mapping a spacetime by a conformal rescaling and compactifying coordinates onto a bounded region of a larger (unphysical) spacetime, so that infinity becomes a boundary whose causal structure can be studied.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried out explicitly for Minkowski space, where the image is a diamond in the Einstein static universe, then asserted for Kruskal.

concepts.name: Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: The static spacetime R x S^3 with metric dt'^2 - dr'^2 - sin^2 r' dOmega^2, pictured as a cylinder whose axis is time and whose cross-sections are unit 3-spheres; it can be embedded as x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2 = 1 in five-dimensional flat space.
concepts.how_introduced: Recognised as the unphysical metric that Minkowski space is conformal to, then described via its cylinder embedding (Fig. 18.7).

concepts.name: 3-sphere
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional analogue of the ordinary sphere: the set of points at unit distance from the origin in four-dimensional Euclidean space, compact and without boundary, coordinatised by r', theta, phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the topology of constant-t' sections of the Einstein static universe, with a promise of more in Part F.

concepts.name: compactified Minkowski spacetime
concepts.definition: The finite region of the Einstein static universe given by |t' +- r'| < pi, r' >= 0, which is conformal to all of Minkowski spacetime; with its boundary it represents Minkowski space together with its points at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after the compactification is completed and shaded on the cylinder in Fig. 18.7.

concepts.name: future and past null infinity
concepts.definition: The null boundary pieces of a conformally compactified asymptotically flat spacetime where outgoing light rays end (scri+) and incoming light rays begin (scri-); in compactified Minkowski they are p = pi/2 and q = -pi/2.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among the boundary components of the Minkowski diamond, with the pronunciation 'scri'.

concepts.name: future and past timelike infinity
concepts.definition: Boundary points of the compactified spacetime where all timelike geodesics end (i+) and begin (i-); in compactified Minkowski i+ is (p, q) = (pi/2, pi/2) and i- is (-pi/2, -pi/2).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed with the other boundary pieces and illustrated by a timelike geodesic from i- to i+ in Fig. 18.8.

concepts.name: spatial infinity
concepts.definition: The boundary point of a compactified asymptotically flat spacetime reached by going to infinite distance along spacelike geodesics; in compactified Minkowski it is (p, q) = (pi/2, -pi/2), a single point though it looks like a circle when one dimension is restored.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed with the other boundary pieces; Fig. 18.8 labels the equatorial rim as i0 'regarded as one point'.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram
concepts.definition: A space-time diagram of a conformally compactified spacetime with angular directions suppressed, drawn so that radial light rays run at 45 degrees and the whole spacetime, including its infinities, fits in a finite figure.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined after compactifying Minkowski space (Fig. 18.9) and then drawn for Kruskal (Fig. 18.10) and collapse (Fig. 18.12).

concepts.name: asymptotically simple spacetime
concepts.definition: Penrose's class of spacetimes that admit a conformal compactification with a regular null boundary at infinity like that of Minkowski space, allowing the same analysis of infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in one sentence as the broad class to which the Minkowski method generalises.
concepts.notes: The book gives no precise definition.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram of the Kruskal spacetime
concepts.definition: A hexagon-shaped conformal diagram with two exterior diamonds (I and I') each carrying i+, i0, i-, scri+ and scri-, a black hole region II above bounded by a horizontal future singularity, and a white hole region II' below bounded by the past singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by applying arctan to scaled Kruskal null coordinates; the computation is omitted and the figure is presented and read.

concepts.name: trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed (compact) spacelike 2-surface for which both the outgoing and the ingoing families of orthogonal light rays converge, so that both wave fronts have smaller area than the surface itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by illuminating a 2-sphere and comparing the areas of the two envelopes of wavelets: normal in region I, trapped in region II, time-reversed trapped in II'.
prerequisites: Penrose diagram of the Kruskal spacetime
concepts.notes: The book prefers Penrose's term to Hawking and Ellis's 'closed trapped surface'. Precise definition uses negative expansions of both null normals.

concepts.name: singularity theorems
concepts.definition: Results showing that, under energy and causality conditions, the existence of a trapped surface forces the spacetime to be null geodesically incomplete, that is, to contain a singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only to explain why trapped surfaces matter.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram of spherical gravitational collapse
concepts.definition: The conformal diagram of a spherical star collapsing to a black hole: a star interior region adjoining the polar axis r = 0, a vacuum exterior bounded by scri- and scri+, an event horizon forming inside the star, trapped surfaces behind it, and a spacelike singularity; no second exterior or white hole appears.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown as the closing figure, compared with the collapse diagrams of Chapter 17.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild in double null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: With both advanced and retarded null coordinates the radial 2-metric has no squared terms; radial light rays are v = const or w = const.
key_equations.symbols: v advanced null coordinate, w retarded null coordinate, r(v, w) areal radius, m mass in geometric units

key_equations.name: Implicit radius
key_equations.meaning: Determines r as a function of the null coordinates.

key_equations.name: Null coordinates from Schwarzschild t
key_equations.latex: v = t + r^*,\qquad w = t - r^*
key_equations.meaning: Symmetric definition of the ingoing and outgoing null coordinates.
key_equations.symbols: t Schwarzschild time, r* tortoise coordinate

key_equations.name: Tortoise coordinate
key_equations.meaning: Radial coordinate in which radial light rays move at unit coordinate speed; diverges logarithmically at the horizon.

key_equations.name: Radial 2-metric
key_equations.meaning: Metric of the theta, phi = const 2-space; conformally flat by the 2D theorem.

key_equations.name: Conformally flat form
key_equations.meaning: Exhibits conformal flatness of the Schwarzschild radial 2-space explicitly.

key_equations.name: Residual freedom of null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Independent relabelling of each null family preserves double null form and changes only the conformal factor; t' = (v'+w')/2, x' = (v'-w')/2.

key_equations.name: Kruskal advanced coordinate
key_equations.meaning: Exponential relabelling of v chosen to cancel the zero of 1 - 2m/r.

key_equations.name: Kruskal retarded coordinate
key_equations.meaning: Companion relabelling of w; the minus sign keeps v' increasing to the future while w' < 0 in region I.

key_equations.name: Kruskal hyperbola relation
key_equations.meaning: Defines r implicitly: r = const curves are hyperbolae, r = 2m is t' = +-x', r = 0 is t'^2 - x'^2 = 2m.

key_equations.name: Kruskal conformal factor
key_equations.meaning: Regular and positive for all r > 0, including r = 2m, which is why the chart crosses the horizon.

key_equations.name: Kruskal line element
key_equations.meaning: Maximal analytic extension of Schwarzschild; radial light rays are 45-degree lines and the only singularity is r = 0.

key_equations.name: Location of the Kruskal singularities (derived from 18.8, not printed)
key_equations.meaning: Two spacelike hyperbolae bounding the spacetime; on the axis x' = 0 they sit at t' = +-(2m)^{1/2}, which is where the bridge pinches off for the normalisation of (18.8).

key_equations.name: Induced metric on t' = 0
key_equations.meaning: Spatial geometry of the Kruskal slice through the bifurcation sphere; r has minimum 2m at x' = 0.

key_equations.name: Equatorial section of the bridge
key_equations.meaning: 2D geometry that is embedded in flat 3-space to draw the Einstein-Rosen bridge.

key_equations.name: Conformal rescaling
key_equations.meaning: Unphysical metric conformal to the physical one; same null geodesics and light cones.
key_equations.symbols: Omega conformal factor, g physical metric, g-bar unphysical metric

key_equations.name: Minkowski null coordinates
key_equations.latex: v = t + r,\qquad w = t - r
key_equations.meaning: Advanced and retarded null coordinates of flat spacetime.

key_equations.name: Minkowski in double null form
key_equations.meaning: Flat metric with r = (v - w)/2.

key_equations.name: Half-plane condition
key_equations.meaning: Only half of the (v, w) plane is physical.

key_equations.name: Arctan compactification
key_equations.meaning: Squeezes each infinite null coordinate into (-pi/2, pi/2).

key_equations.name: Compactified half-plane
key_equations.meaning: Image of r >= 0.

key_equations.name: Minkowski after compactification
key_equations.meaning: Flat metric written as a conformal factor times a regular metric on a finite coordinate domain.

key_equations.name: Unphysical metric
key_equations.meaning: Rescaled metric regular at p, q = +-pi/2; Omega^2 = 4 cos^2 p cos^2 q vanishes on the boundary at infinity.

key_equations.name: Time and radius on the cylinder
key_equations.latex: t' = p + q,\qquad r' = p - q
key_equations.meaning: Converts null coordinates back to time-like and space-like ones.

key_equations.name: Range of compactified Minkowski
key_equations.meaning: Diamond-shaped region (a triangle in the r' >= 0 half) that is the image of all of Minkowski spacetime.

key_equations.name: Einstein static universe metric
key_equations.meaning: The unphysical metric is the ESU; Minkowski is conformal to a finite part of it.
key_equations.symbols: t' cylinder time, r' polar angle on S^3

key_equations.name: Full ESU coordinate range
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates on R x S^3; r' = 0, pi and theta = 0, pi are coordinate singularities.

key_equations.name: Cylinder embedding of the ESU
key_equations.meaning: Realises the ESU as a cylinder in flat 5D space of signature -3.
key_equations.symbols: here w is a fifth Cartesian coordinate, not the null coordinate

key_equations.name: Boundary of compactified Minkowski
key_equations.meaning: Conformal infinity decomposed into two null surfaces and three points.

key_equations.name: Kruskal compactification
key_equations.meaning: Arctan applied to scaled Kruskal null coordinates, giving the Penrose diagram Fig. 18.10.

key_equations.name: Printed range for the Kruskal compactification (needs correction)
key_equations.meaning: As printed, the third inequality follows from the first two and does not cut off the singularities. Since v'w' = t'^2 - x'^2 and r = 0 at v'w' = 2m, the singularities lie at tan v'' tan w'' = 1, i.e. v'' + w'' = +-pi/2; the physical range is -pi/2 < v'' + w'' < pi/2, which gives the hexagon of Fig. 18.10.

figures.label: Fig. 18.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Kruskal spacetime drawn in the (t', x') plane with angular directions suppressed.
figures.visual_description: Vertical t' axis and horizontal x' axis cross at the centre. Two heavy diagonal lines through the origin are the horizons, labelled r = 2m with t = +infinity on the upper-left branch and t = -infinity on the lower-left. Families of hyperbolae: on the right (region I) curves labelled r = 3m and r = 4m open to the right; mirror curves labelled r = 4m and r = 3m sit on the left (region I'); near the top and bottom, curves labelled r = m lie just inside wavy hyperbolic boundaries marked 'Future singularity r = 0' (top) and 'Past singularity r = 0' (bottom), with horizontal hatching beyond them marking the excluded region. Thin straight lines through the origin in region I carry labels t = 2m, t = m, t = 0 (along the x' axis), t = -m, t = -2m. Roman numerals I, I', II and II' sit in the four wedges, and a handful of small upright 45-degree light cones are scattered over the diagram (in I and I', in II, and near the upper-left r = 3m and r = 4m curves), all identical in shape. A curve labelled 'Radially infalling particle' starts at the r = 4m hyperbola on the x' axis with a light cone, rises and bends left across the horizon into region II and reaches the future singularity; parallel dashed 45-degree lines labelled 'Escaping signals' leave its early worldline toward the upper right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Kruskal coordinates make every light cone a 45-degree cone, turn r = constant into hyperbolae and the horizon into straight null lines, reveal four regions including a second exterior, and show that signals from the infalling particle escape only before it crosses r = 2m while the spacelike future singularity is unavoidable.

redesign.idea: Live Kruskal diagram coupled to a Schwarzschild-coordinate panel: the same worldline and light signals drawn in (t, r) and in (t', x'), with coordinate grids of constant r (hyperbolae) and constant t (rays through the origin).
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a release radius and emission times; the infalling worldline is integrated and drawn in both panels, each emitted photon is traced at 45 degrees and coloured green if it reaches large r or red if it hits r = 0. A toggle highlights each region I, II, I', II' and names its EF chart; hovering a point reports r, t and which light rays from it escape.

figures.label: Fig. 18.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Embedding picture of the Einstein-Rosen bridge on the slice t' = 0.
figures.visual_description: A perspective drawing of two roughly horizontal curved sheets, one above the other, each flaring into a funnel that meets the other at a narrow circular throat in the middle. A grid covers the sheets: concentric circles around the throat and radial lines running out from it. Labels above point to the radial lines as 'phi = constant' and to the circles as 'x' = constant'. The outer parts of both sheets flatten out.
figures.what_it_teaches: At the instant t' = 0 the Kruskal geometry consists of two asymptotically flat spaces connected by a minimal sphere of radius 2m.

redesign.idea: 3D embedding surface of the t' = 0 equatorial slice (the two-sided Flamm paraboloid) with a synchronized marker on the Kruskal diagram.
redesign.interaction: Learner moves a point along the x' axis of a small Kruskal inset; the corresponding circle lights up on the 3D surface with its radius r and proper distance from the throat displayed. Orbit, zoom and a switch to show proper-distance ticks along a radial grid line.

figures.label: Fig. 18.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Seven schematic profiles showing how the bridge evolves in Kruskal time.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal strip of seven boxes labelled beneath: t' < -1, t' = -1, -1 < t' < 0, t' = 0, 0 < t' < 1, t' = 1, t' > 1. The outer boxes show two separate curves bending toward each other without touching (two disconnected sheets with cusps). At t' = +-1 the two curves meet at a single point. Between, the curves form a pair of facing arcs like ')(' whose gap is widest in the t' = 0 box and narrower in the neighbouring boxes. Each profile is meant to be spun about a vertical axis to recover a surface.
figures.what_it_teaches: The bridge is not static: the throat opens from nothing, reaches its maximum radius 2m at t' = 0 and closes again, with the two universes separated before and after, symmetric in time.
concepts: dynamical pinch-off of the Einstein-Rosen bridge

redesign.idea: Animated 3D bridge surface driven by a Kruskal-time slider, next to a Kruskal diagram showing the chosen t' = constant line crossing the singularity hyperbolae.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs t'; the embedded slice surface morphs (throat radius shown numerically) and the slice line moves in the Kruskal diagram. A 'send a photon' button launches a light ray from region I toward I' and shows it strike the singularity before the throat can be crossed.

figures.label: Fig. 18.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A wormhole joining two far-apart parts of one universe.
figures.visual_description: A single flat sheet folded back on itself like a hairpin: a rounded fold on the left joins an upper and a lower layer. In the middle a vertical tube connects a funnel opening in the upper layer to one in the lower layer; both funnel mouths carry grids of concentric circles and radial lines, and the tube carries vertical and horizontal grid lines.
figures.what_it_teaches: The same local slice geometry as the bridge can belong to a manifold with different topology, where the throat links distant regions of one asymptotically flat space.

redesign.idea: Side-by-side 3D surfaces with identical throat geometry: two separate sheets versus one folded sheet, with a path-length comparison.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags two points on the outer sheet(s) and compares the path through the throat with the path through the exterior; a toggle switches topology while leaving local grids unchanged.

figures.label: Fig. 18.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Graph of the inverse tangent, which maps the whole real line onto an interval of length pi.
figures.visual_description: Horizontal x axis and vertical axis labelled tan^-1 x. A smooth increasing S-shaped curve through the origin approaches dashed horizontal asymptotes marked pi/2 above and -pi/2 below.
figures.what_it_teaches: The basic trick of compactification: a monotonic function can relabel an infinite range by a finite one without losing ordering.

redesign.idea: Number line squeezer: a long ruler of equally spaced ticks is mapped through arctan onto a finite segment.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a point to large x and watches its image crowd toward pi/2; a toggle compares arctan with tanh and with x/(1+|x|) to show the choice of squeezing function is not unique.

figures.label: Fig. 18.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Ordinary spacetime diagram of Minkowski space in (t, r).
figures.visual_description: Vertical t axis at the left edge and horizontal r axis, only r >= 0 drawn. A lattice of criss-crossing straight lines at 45 degrees fills the half-plane; labels with pointer lines mark one family as w = constant (rising to the right) and the other as v = constant (falling to the right).
figures.what_it_teaches: In flat space the null coordinates v and w label two families of radial light rays, and r >= 0 restricts to half the (v, w) plane.

redesign.idea: Combined with Fig. 18.9 as a morphing animation (see that entry).
redesign.interaction: Grid of null lines with draggable labels v and w that update as the pointer moves.

figures.label: Fig. 18.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Minkowski spacetime as a finite region drawn on the Einstein static universe cylinder, with two dimensions suppressed.
figures.visual_description: A vertical cylinder with three horizontal elliptical cross-sections labelled t' = pi (top), t' = 0 and t' = -pi. The generator on the left is labelled r' = 0 and the one on the right r' = pi. A band shaded with vertical hatching wraps around the cylinder surface: its lower boundary curve (partly dashed on the far side) runs from a point i- near t' = -pi on r' = 0 up to a dot i0 at t' = 0 on the far side, labelled scri- ; its upper boundary runs from i0 up to i+ near t' = pi on r' = 0, labelled scri+.
figures.what_it_teaches: All of Minkowski space occupies a bounded patch of the static cylinder; its infinity becomes an honest boundary consisting of two null surfaces and three points.

redesign.idea: 3D Einstein cylinder (one space dimension, the (t', r') slice extended around the circle) with the Minkowski patch painted on and light rays drawn as helices at 45 degrees.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a Minkowski event and a null ray in a flat inset; the image point and ray appear on the rotating cylinder. A slider shrinks the physical region to show how larger and larger Minkowski balls fill the diamond and approach its edges.

figures.label: Fig. 18.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Where timelike, null and spacelike geodesics start and end in compactified Minkowski space, with one dimension suppressed.
figures.visual_description: Two cones joined base to base, apex i+ at the top and i- at the bottom, drawn with a vertical axis line labelled r = 0. The wide common rim is labelled i0 (regarded as one point). The upper conical surface is labelled scri+, the lower scri-; smaller horizontal ellipses drawn on the cone surfaces are cuts of null infinity, labelled q = constant (on the upper cone) and p = constant (on the lower cone). A curved line with an arrow runs from i- to i+ labelled 'Timelike geodesic'; a straight line from the lower cone to the upper cone is labelled 'Null geodesic'; an arrowed arc across the rim ellipse is labelled 'Spacelike geodesic'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Timelike geodesics run from i- to i+, null geodesics from scri- to scri+, spacelike geodesics from i0 back to i0; the rim, though drawn as a circle, is a single point of the conformal boundary.

redesign.idea: 3D double-cone conformal boundary with launchable geodesics of each causal type.
redesign.interaction: Learner picks an event and a velocity (timelike, null or spacelike direction) in a physical Minkowski inset; the geodesic is mapped and drawn inside the double cone, with its two endpoints highlighted on i+-, scri+- or i0. A contrasting 'accelerated rocket' option shows a non-geodesic curve ending on scri+ instead of i+.

figures.label: Fig. 18.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of Minkowski spacetime with two dimensions suppressed.
figures.visual_description: A triangle with a vertical left edge labelled r = 0 running from i- (bottom) to i+ (top), and a right-hand vertex i0. The upper slanted edge is labelled scri+, the lower slanted edge scri-. Inside, one family of curves (labelled t = constant) runs from the r = 0 edge to converge on i0, nearly horizontal in the middle and bending up or down near the top and bottom; the other family (labelled r = constant) runs from i- to i+, bowing out toward i0.
figures.what_it_teaches: The whole of flat spacetime fits in a finite triangle whose edges are the different infinities; surfaces of constant t all meet at spatial infinity and worldlines of constant r all meet at timelike infinity.

redesign.idea: Morph animation from the ordinary Minkowski (t, r) grid (Fig. 18.6) to the Penrose triangle, driven by a parameter that blends identity into the arctan map.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs the morph slider and watches constant-t and constant-r lines bend while the 45-degree null lines stay straight; clicking any grid line highlights it in both pictures and shows its equation in (t', r').

figures.caption_paraphrase: Uncaptioned decorative element: a blank ruled grid in the page margin.
figures.visual_description: A tall narrow grid of empty rectangular cells, two columns wide and many rows high, with no labels or content. The renders of pdf pages 366 and 367 show this grid printed in the outer page margin (note space), separate from any figure.
figures.what_it_teaches: Nothing about physics; it is a page-design element (note space) of this edition.

figures.label: Fig. 18.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of the maximally extended Schwarzschild (Kruskal) spacetime.
figures.visual_description: A horizontally elongated hexagon. The top edge is a horizontal wavy line labelled 'Future singularity r = 0' running between two vertices labelled i+; the bottom edge is a wavy 'Past singularity r = 0' between two vertices labelled i-. The far left and far right vertices are labelled i0. The four slanted outer edges are labelled scri+ (upper) and scri- (lower) on each side. Two diagonals cross at the centre, dividing the figure into regions labelled I (right), I' (left), II (top) and II' (bottom). In I and I' lens-shaped curves of constant r run from i- to i+ bulging toward i0, and curves of constant t fan from the central crossing to i0; in II and II' gently curved lines stretch between the singularity vertices and lines fan from the centre to the singularity.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each exterior region is a copy of the Minkowski triangle with its own infinities; the horizons are 45-degree lines; the singularities are spacelike; from outside r = 2m an outgoing radial ray reaches scri+ but an ingoing one hits the singularity, and from inside both hit it.
concepts: Penrose diagram of the Kruskal spacetime

redesign.idea: Linked triple view: Schwarzschild (t, r) chart, Kruskal diagram, and Penrose hexagon, sharing a cursor.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks any event; its future and past radial light rays are drawn in all three views and their end points (scri+, future singularity, etc.) are named. A region-highlight toggle shows which parts each chart covers, and a slider draws constant-r or constant-t curves to connect the pictures.

figures.label: Fig. 18.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: Wave fronts from a 2-sphere S0 that emits a flash of light.
figures.visual_description: Three concentric circles labelled S1 (innermost), S0 (middle) and S2 (outermost). Three small circles are centred on points of S0 (at left, upper right and lower right), each marked by a dot at its centre and touching both S1 and S2, illustrating that S1 and S2 are the inner and outer envelopes of wavelets from S0.
figures.what_it_teaches: A flashing sphere produces an ingoing and an outgoing wave front; comparing their areas with S0 tests whether the sphere is normal, trapped or anti-trapped.

redesign.idea: Huygens-envelope animator for a flashing sphere placed in region I, II or II' of the Kruskal geometry.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the sphere's position on a Penrose diagram; the panel animates wavelets and shows the two envelope areas as bars versus the area of S0, flipping the label between normal, trapped and anti-trapped as the horizon is crossed.

figures.label: Fig. 18.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram for a spherical star collapsing to a black hole.
figures.visual_description: A roughly triangular region. The vertical left edge is labelled 'Polar origin r = 0'. A diagonally hatched strip labelled 'Star interior' hugs that edge; its right boundary (the star's surface) curves up from the bottom vertex and meets the top edge near the top-left corner. The top edge is a short horizontal wavy line labelled 'Singularity r = 0'. A dashed 45-degree segment labelled 'Event horizon r = 2m' starts on the star's surface a little below the singularity and runs up to the right-hand end of the wavy line, the unlabelled corner where the slanted outer edge begins. A dot just under the singularity, between the star surface and the dashed horizon, is labelled 'Trapped surface'. The unshaded region to the right is labelled 'Empty space'; its outer boundary descends from the top-right corner to a right-hand vertex (scri+) and returns to the bottom vertex (scri-).
figures.what_it_teaches: Realistic collapse produces a horizon, trapped surfaces and a spacelike singularity, but only a single exterior; the second universe and white hole of Kruskal are replaced by the star.
concepts: Penrose diagram of spherical gravitational collapse

redesign.idea: Build-a-collapse diagram: start from the Kruskal hexagon and paste in a star surface worldline to cut away regions I' and II'.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the star's surface worldline (initial radius, start time); the diagram recomputes which parts of Kruskal survive, draws the event horizon backward from where the surface crosses r = 2m and marks where trapped spheres first appear.

worked_examples.problem: Find coordinates in which the Schwarzschild metric is regular across both the future and past horizons and radial light rays are straight.
worked_examples.method: Write the radial 2-metric in double null form (1 - 2m/r) dv dw; note that separate relabellings of v and w keep the null form; pick v' = exp(v/4m), w' = -exp(-w/4m); compute the product v'w' in terms of r and the Jacobian factor; define t', x' as half sum and difference.
worked_examples.key_insight: The exponential Jacobian vanishes exactly as fast as 1 - 2m/r near the horizon, so their ratio, the new conformal factor, stays finite and positive.

worked_examples.problem: Follow the radial timelike geodesic that the text starts at r = 4m on the slice t' = 0, together with the outward light signals it emits.
worked_examples.method: Draw the worldline in the Kruskal diagram using the 45-degree light cones; send outgoing 45-degree signals from successive points.
worked_examples.key_insight: Signals sent before the particle crosses the diagonal r = 2m reach large r; later signals are confined to region II and end on the spacelike singularity along with the particle.
worked_examples.result: Qualitative: finite proper time to r = 0, escape cut off at the horizon.

worked_examples.problem: Determine the spatial geometry of the Kruskal slice t' = 0.
worked_examples.method: Set dt' = 0 in (18.9) to get (18.10); set t' = 0 in (18.8) so that -(r - 2m)e^{r/2m} = -x'^2, and see that r decreases from infinity to 2m as x' goes to 0 and then increases again; restrict to the equator and embed.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because r has a minimum rather than reaching zero on this slice, the slice joins two exterior regions through a smallest sphere.
worked_examples.result: Two asymptotically flat sheets linked by a throat of radius 2m (Fig. 18.2); later slices have narrower throats and pinch off at the singularity.

worked_examples.method: Use v = t + r, w = t - r to get dv dw - (v - w)^2 dOmega^2/4 with v >= w; set p = arctan v, q = arctan w and use dv = sec^2 p dp and v - w = sin(p - q) sec p sec q to factor out sec^2 p sec^2 q /4; define t' = p + q, r' = p - q.
worked_examples.key_insight: After factoring, what remains is a perfectly regular metric that is recognisably the Einstein static universe, defined on a bounded range; the conformal factor carries all the infinity.

worked_examples.problem: Identify the boundary of compactified Minkowski space and where geodesics of each type begin and end.
worked_examples.method: Take the limits p -> +-pi/2, q -> +-pi/2 allowed by p >= q; classify the resulting sets as null segments or points; follow straight lines t = t0 + u r (|u| < 1, = 1, > 1) through the arctan map.
worked_examples.key_insight: Different causal types of geodesic reach infinity at different parts of the boundary, so 'infinity' in a Lorentzian spacetime has structure.
worked_examples.result: scri+ at p = pi/2, scri- at q = -pi/2, i+ at (pi/2, pi/2), i0 at (pi/2, -pi/2), i- at (-pi/2, -pi/2); timelike from i- to i+, null from scri- to scri+, spacelike from i0 to i0.

worked_examples.problem: Read from the Kruskal Penrose diagram where radial light rays from a given event end.
worked_examples.method: Draw both 45-degree lines through the event in Fig. 18.10 and see which boundary edge each meets first.
worked_examples.key_insight: Outside the horizon one ray reaches scri+ and the other the singularity; inside, both lines meet the horizontal singularity because it lies entirely to the future.
concepts: Penrose diagram of the Kruskal spacetime

worked_examples.problem: Decide whether a round 2-sphere in each Kruskal region is trapped.
worked_examples.method: Flash the sphere, construct the inner and outer envelopes of the wavelets (Fig. 18.11), and compare their areas 4 pi r^2 with that of the original sphere, using the direction in which r must change along each null direction in the region.
worked_examples.key_insight: Trapping is about both null directions reducing area, which in region II follows because r must decrease along every future-directed causal direction.
worked_examples.result: Region I: outer front larger, inner smaller (normal). Region II: both smaller (trapped). Region II': both larger (time-reversed trapped).

worked_examples.problem: Show that convergence of light rays in both directions does not by itself make a surface trapped.
worked_examples.method: Take two past light cones in Minkowski space and intersect them; check that the wave fronts from the intersection converge but that the surface is not closed.
worked_examples.key_insight: Compactness is essential to trapping; an unbounded convergent surface exists even in flat spacetime.
worked_examples.result: The intersection is convergent but not trapped, which is why the authors see no need for the adjective 'closed'.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Squeezing the whole real line into a finite interval with arctan
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Shows in one graph that relabelling can bring 'infinity' to a finite coordinate value while preserving order, which is then applied to each null coordinate.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A coordinate change alone cannot make distances finite; a conformal factor must also be discarded, and the arctan choice is not unique.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Rubber ruler: stretch-and-squeeze animation of evenly spaced ticks under arctan, then applied to both axes of a light-cone grid.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Each point of the 2D diagram is really a whole sphere
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reminds readers that the Kruskal and Penrose diagrams hide 2-spheres of area 4 pi r^2, which is needed for the bridge and trapped-surface arguments.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only valid for spherically symmetric spacetimes; the sphere's radius differs from point to point.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Hover any diagram point to pop up a 3D sphere scaled to its r.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Rotating a profile curve about an axis to generate a surface
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The seven flat profiles in Fig. 18.3 become surfaces of revolution, turning a cheap strip of drawings into a movie of the throat.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Embedding pictures show slice geometry only; the evolution depends on how slices are chosen and does not show causal structure.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Lathe tool: learner spins a profile to build the throat surface and scrubs time.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A cylinder x^2 + y^2 = 1 in 3D as a stand-in for the Einstein static universe
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Suppressing two dimensions, the 3-sphere cross-section becomes a circle and the ESU becomes an ordinary cylinder with time along its length.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The cylinder is drawn in Euclidean space, but the relevant geometry is Lorentzian; the book's parenthetical even writes the signature with opposite sign.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The 3-sphere as the next member of the family circle, 2-sphere, ...
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Lets readers accept S^3 cross-sections of the ESU without formal topology.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Visual intuition fails in three dimensions; poles r' = 0, pi are coordinate artefacts.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Stereographic slicing of S^3 into nested 2-spheres controlled by r'.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Huygens wavelets from a flashing sphere form an inner and an outer wave front
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Turns the abstract condition on null expansions into a picture of two envelopes whose areas can be compared with the original sphere.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The flat-picture intuition that the outer front is always bigger is exactly what fails in region II; the picture itself does not show why.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Flash-the-sphere animation with area bars that change sign across the horizon.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A folded sheet with a tube connecting two layers
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Keeps the throat geometry identical while changing how the far regions connect, making vivid that field equations do not fix topology.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The folded embedding is not a vacuum solution with time evolution; it is a static cartoon of one slice.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Eddington-Finkelstein charts straighten one family of radial light rays; Kruskal straightens both at once
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Presents the Kruskal construction as completing a job the previous chapter did halfway.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Straightness of null lines is chart dependent and does not by itself guarantee regularity; the conformal factor must also be finite.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Three-panel comparison: Schwarzschild, advanced EF, Kruskal, with the same light rays drawn.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A maximal spacetime must be free of singularities (maximal and geodesically complete mean the same thing).
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Maximality allows geodesics to end at intrinsic singularities; completeness forbids any end. Kruskal is maximal but incomplete.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both notions are phrased in terms of extending geodesics to infinite affine parameter.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Einstein's equations determine the topology of spacetime, so the Kruskal region I' must exist wherever a black hole exists.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Field equations are local and fix geometry near each point; different global manifolds can share it, and the physical status of I' is open (and in collapse it is absent).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Kruskal is presented as the unique maximal analytic extension, which sounds like physical necessity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Einstein-Rosen bridge is a static tunnel through which one could travel from region I to region I'.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The throat opens and closes in Kruskal time; it pinches off when slices reach the singularity, and any causal path from I into the throat ends in region II before reaching I'.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The single t' = 0 embedding picture looks like a permanent static tube.
concepts: dynamical pinch-off of the Einstein-Rosen bridge

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The future singularity at r = 0 is a point at the centre that an infalling observer might steer around.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In Kruskal and Penrose diagrams r = 0 is spacelike, a moment in the future of every event in region II, so it cannot be avoided.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In flat-space intuition r = 0 is a location in space.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Penrose diagrams preserve distances or times, so the size of a region indicates how big it is.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The conformal factor distorts lengths enormously (near the boundary Omega goes to zero); only light-cone directions and causal relations are faithful.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: They look like ordinary spacetime diagrams with coordinates.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every timelike curve ends at i+ and every lightlike-looking curve ends on scri+.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The endpoint rules hold for geodesics; a uniformly accelerated observer, for example, asymptotes to a null direction and ends on scri+ rather than i+.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The rules are stated crisply and seem to classify all curves.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Spatial infinity i0 is a circle (or sphere) because it is drawn as the rim of a double cone.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the compactification all spacelike directions reach the same point i0; the rim is an artefact of drawing one extra dimension.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Fig. 18.8 shows the rim as a large ellipse.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any surface whose light rays converge in both directions is trapped.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The surface must also be closed; the intersection of two past light cones in Minkowski space converges both ways but is not trapped.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Convergence is the part of the definition that seems physically decisive.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A real astrophysical black hole contains a white hole in its past and a second universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Penrose diagram of collapse (Fig. 18.12) replaces regions I' and II' with the star interior; they belong only to the idealised eternal vacuum solution.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The maximal extension is presented first and at length, so it is easy to treat it as the generic black hole.
concepts: Penrose diagram of spherical gravitational collapse

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because Kruskal diagrams have 45-degree light cones everywhere, spacetime is flat in these coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the radial 2-metric is conformally flat; curvature is carried by the non-constant conformal factor and by r(t', x').
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Straight 45-degree null lines are the hallmark of Minkowski diagrams.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The horizon r = 2m is a singular place where something physically breaks down.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In Kruskal coordinates the metric is regular there; the horizon is a pair of straight null lines crossing at a regular 2-sphere.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Schwarzschild coordinates the metric blows up at r = 2m.

thought_experiments.name: Signals from an infalling particle
thought_experiments.setup: A particle on a radial geodesic starting at r = 4m, t' = 0 in region I (drawn as if it begins at rest) keeps emitting outward light pulses as it approaches and crosses r = 2m.
thought_experiments.lesson: Pulses before the horizon crossing escape to distant observers; pulses after it are trapped in region II and end on the singularity with the emitter.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Kruskal-diagram signal launcher with escape/no-escape colouring.

thought_experiments.name: Meeting a visitor from the other universe
thought_experiments.setup: An observer in region I and one in region I' each decide to meet the other (posed as Exercise 18.4).
thought_experiments.lesson: They can only meet inside the black hole region II, and both then end at the future singularity; the two exteriors never exchange signals.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Two-player Penrose-diagram game where each player steers a worldline and the app shows the earliest possible meeting point and its fate.

thought_experiments.name: Trying to cross the Einstein-Rosen bridge
thought_experiments.setup: Picture a light ray sent from region I toward the throat seen on the t' = 0 slice, aiming for region I'.
thought_experiments.lesson: The throat closes before the ray can pass through; crossing would need a spacelike path, so the bridge is non-traversable.
concepts: dynamical pinch-off of the Einstein-Rosen bridge
thought_experiments.app_idea: Race animation: throat radius versus photon position on successive slices.

thought_experiments.name: Flashing a sphere
thought_experiments.setup: Light is emitted from every point of a 2-sphere at one instant, first in region I, then in region II, then in region II'.
thought_experiments.lesson: Whether the two resulting wave fronts grow or shrink diagnoses normal, trapped, and anti-trapped surfaces, the key input to singularity theorems.

thought_experiments.name: A shortcut between distant places
thought_experiments.setup: Identify the two sheets of the bridge as far-apart regions of one universe (Fig. 18.4).
thought_experiments.lesson: Identical local geometry can have different global topology; Einstein's equations alone cannot tell which is realised.

historical_notes.event: Found the maximal analytic extension of the Schwarzschild solution by straightening both families of radial null geodesics; the book credits him alone and asserts uniqueness.
historical_notes.significance: Settled the global structure of the eternal Schwarzschild black hole and introduced the second exterior region and white hole. George Szekeres found the same extension independently, which the book does not mention.

historical_notes.event: Their name is attached to the throat connecting two exterior sheets of the Schwarzschild geometry.
historical_notes.significance: The Einstein-Rosen bridge is the prototype of a wormhole and of the question whether mathematically allowed topology is physical.

historical_notes.event: Introduced conformal compactification, the diagrams that bear his name, the notion of simple (asymptotically simple) spacetimes, and the term 'trapped surface'.
historical_notes.significance: Made infinity and causal structure tractable and supplied the concept that drives the singularity theorems.

historical_notes.event: Their monograph The Large Scale Structure of Space-Time is named as the main source for the chapter; the authors also contrast their term 'closed trapped surface' with Penrose's.
historical_notes.significance: Standard reference for global methods in GR.

applications_and_observations.topic: Spherical collapse of a star to a black hole
applications_and_observations.details: The Penrose diagram of collapse shows that a realistic black hole formed from a star has one exterior, an event horizon that forms inside the star before its surface crosses r = 2m, trapped surfaces behind the horizon, and a spacelike singularity; the idealised second universe and white hole are absent.

applications_and_observations.topic: Lifetime of the Einstein-Rosen throat (own estimate, not in the text)
applications_and_observations.details: The throat centre follows a radial geodesic released from rest at r = 2m, whose proper time to r = 0 is pi m; a signal cannot cross in that time, so the bridge is non-traversable.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: tau = pi GM/c^3; for one solar mass about 1.5e-5 s (m = 1.48 km).

applications_and_observations.topic: Proper time for the infalling particle of Fig. 18.1 (own estimate, not in the text)
applications_and_observations.details: Assuming the particle of Fig. 18.1 starts from rest (the text only says it starts at r = 4m, t' = 0), radial free fall from rest at r0 reaches r = 0 after proper time (pi/2) r0^(3/2)/(2m)^(1/2) in geometric units; with r0 = 4m this is about 8.9m.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: About 8.9 GM/c^3, roughly 4.4e-5 s for a solar-mass hole or about 12 hours for a 1e9 solar-mass hole.

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of the bridge throat (own estimate, not in the text)
applications_and_observations.details: On t' = 0 the minimal sphere has r = 2m, so its area is 16 pi m^2, the horizon area of the black hole.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Area about 110 km^2 for one solar mass (r = 2.95 km).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Book uses signature (+, -, -, -), so timelike intervals have ds^2 > 0 and spatial slices carry negative-definite induced metrics as in (18.10)-(18.11).
notation_and_conventions.notes: The parenthetical cylinder metric on p.350 is written with the opposite overall sign (-dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2); treat it as a slip.

notation_and_conventions.convention: A flat 5D metric with one plus and four minus signs is described as having signature -3 (sum of the diagonal signs).
Geometric units with G = c = 1; m is the mass parameter (GM/c^2) and the horizon is at r = 2m.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Logarithms of dimensional quantities such as ln(r - 2m) implicitly fix a length unit; t' = +-1 as pinch-off time also presupposes a choice of units.

notation_and_conventions.convention: v advanced (ingoing, constant on ingoing radial light rays), w retarded (outgoing). Primes mark Kruskal relabellings v', w'; double primes v'', w'' mark their compactified versions.
t' = (v' + w')/2 and x' = (v' - w')/2; Kruskal regions are labelled I (our exterior), II (black hole), I' (other exterior), II' (white hole).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other books use U, V or T, X, and label regions I-IV differently.

notation_and_conventions.convention: t' is reused in §18.4 for the Einstein static universe time p + q and r' for p - q, unrelated to the Kruskal t', x' of §18.2; w is also reused as a fifth Cartesian coordinate in the ESU embedding.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Rename in teaching materials (e.g. T, X for Kruskal; tau, chi for ESU).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Physical metric g_ab, unphysical metric g-bar_ab = Omega^2 g_ab; for Minkowski Omega^-2 = (1/4) sec^2 p sec^2 q.
Script I (pronounced 'scri') with + or - for future or past null infinity; i+, i- for timelike infinity; i0 for spatial infinity.
The book writes d theta^2 + sin^2 theta d phi^2 explicitly; this dossier abbreviates it as dOmega^2.

margin_notes.summary: Aside that r* is known by some authors as the tortoise radial coordinate.
Parenthetical warning that the geodesic endpoint rules for i+-, scri+- and i0 do not apply to non-geodesic curves.
Promise that the Einstein static universe and the 3-sphere will be treated properly in Part F on cosmology.
Instruction to rotate each profile of the bridge evolution strip about its vertical axis to recover the 2D surfaces.
Terminology note preferring Penrose's 'trapped surface' to Hawking and Ellis's 'closed trapped surface', backed by a Minkowski counterexample showing convergence without closure is not trapping.
